maths_eduqas_f.1.5.summary: This revision note covers the vital algebraic distinction between equations, which are only true for specific values of the unknown, and identities, which are true for all values of the variable. You will learn how to formally prove that two expressions are identically equivalent using algebraic manipulation and expansion. Master these foundational concepts to secure full marks on algebraic proof and verification questions in both non-calculator and calculator papers.

core.p: Algebraic language relies on precise definitions to distinguish between expressions, equations, and identities. Understanding these distinctions is crucial for proper algebraic manipulation and proof.
bullets: An expression is a collection of terms, numbers, and variables with no equals sign.
An equation contains an equals sign and is only true for specific values of the variable.
An identity is true for every single value of the variable and uses the triple-bar symbol.

callouts.p: An identity is a mathematical statement that is true for all possible values of the variables involved, denoted by the symbol \u2261.
Never use an equals sign (=) when writing an identity if the question specifically tests the difference, though standard textbooks sometimes blur this.

fig.cap: Comparison of an expression, equation, and identity showing their distinct symbols and meanings.
fig.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 240"><rect x="10" y="20" width="115" height="200" rx="10" fill="#dbeafe" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="20" y="45" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#1b2540">Expression</text><text x="20" y="80" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">3x + 5</text><text x="20" y="120" font-size="11" fill="#475569">No equals sign.</text><text x="20" y="145" font-size="11" fill="#475569">Cannot be solved.</text><rect x="142" y="20" width="115" height="200" rx="10" fill="#fde68a" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="152" y="45" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#1b2540">Equation</text><text x="152" y="80" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">3x + 5 = 14</text><text x="152" y="120" font-size="11" fill="#475569">True for x = 3</text><text x="152" y="145" font-size="11" fill="#475569">Only one solution.</text><rect x="274" y="20" width="115" height="200" rx="10" fill="#bbf7d0" stroke="#1b2540" stroke-width="2"/><text x="284" y="45" font-size="14" font-weight="bold" fill="#1b2540">Identity</text><text x="284" y="80" font-size="12" fill="#1b2540">3(x+1) \u2261 3x+3</text><text x="284" y="120" font-size="11" fill="#475569">True for all x.</text><text x="284" y="145" font-size="11" fill="#475569">Always balanced.</text></svg>

core.p: An equation is a mathematical statement asserting that two expressions are equal. It acts like a weighing scale that balances only for specific numerical inputs.
bullets: Contains an equals sign (=).
Can be solved to find the unknown value.
Example: 2x + 7 = 15 is only true when x = 4.
Substituting any other number into x makes the left side unequal to the right side.

callouts.p: Linear equations typically have one unique solution, whereas quadratic equations can have two solutions.

core.p: An identity means that the left-hand side and right-hand side are identical in value for every conceivable number substituted in. It is an algebraic fact rather than a puzzle to solve.
bullets: Uses the symbol \u2261 instead of =.
Demonstrates that two expressions are completely equivalent after simplification.
Testing \u2261 with x = 2 gives: (2+3)^2 = 25, and 2^2 + 6(2) + 9 = 4 + 12 + 9 = 25. Both sides match.

callouts.p: If an exam question asks if a statement is an identity, test at least two different numbers (e.g., x = 0 and x = 2). If they match, it is likely an identity, but you must prove it algebraically.

core.p: Students often confuse solving an equation with verifying an identity. It is vital to understand the conceptual difference behind the notation.
bullets: Equations ask: 'For what value of x is this true?'
Identities state: 'This is always true, regardless of x.'
Equations can have no solutions, one solution, or multiple solutions.
Identities have infinitely many solutions because every number works.

core.p: To argue that two expressions are equivalent, you must manipulate one side algebraically until it looks exactly like the other side, or simplify both sides independently until they match.
bullets: Expand all brackets on both sides.
Collect all like terms on each side separately.
Compare the coefficient of each power of x.
Conclude with a clear statement that the expressions are equivalent.

callouts.p: Two polynomial expressions are identical if and only if the coefficients of corresponding powers of x are equal.

core.p: Single and double bracket expansions are the primary tool for showing that a factored expression is equivalent to an expanded quadratic or cubic expression.
bullets: Single brackets: a(bx + c) \u2261 abx + ac.
Double brackets: (x + a)(x + b) \u2261 x^2 + (a+b)x + ab.
Always check sign rules carefully when expanding negative terms.

callouts.p: Never write (x + 3)^2 \u2261 x^2 + 9. You must include the middle term 6x.

core.p: Conversely, you can prove equivalence by factorising an expanded expression to show it matches a factored form.
bullets: Look for common numerical and algebraic factors.
Use difference of two squares: a^2 - b^2 \u2261 (a - b)(a + b).
Factorise quadratic expressions into two brackets.

core.p: While you cannot prove an identity by substitution alone (since matching numbers could happen by coincidence), you can easily disprove an identity with a single counterexample.
bullets: If left side \u2260 right side for even one value of x, it is NOT an identity.
Choose easy numbers like x = 0, x = 1, or x = -1 to test quickly.
State your substitution clearly and show the numerical evaluations.

callouts.p: Substitution is your best weapon for disprove questions on non-calculator papers.

core.h: 9. Working with Missing Coefficients in Identities
core.p: Higher foundation questions often feature an identity with an unknown letter (like p or q) and ask you to find its value.
bullets: Given: 5x + 12 \u2261 a(x + 2) + b, find a and b.
Expand the right side: ax + 2a + b.
Equate coefficients of x: a = 5.
Equate constant terms: 2a + b = 12, so 2(5) + b = 12 \u21d2 b = 2.

core.p: Eduqas papers use specific phrasing that dictates how much working you must show when dealing with equations and identities.
bullets: 'Solve': Find the value of x in an equation.
'Show that': Prove step-by-step that an equivalence is true.
'Verify': Check by substitution that a statement holds true.
'Explain why': Write a brief mathematical sentence justifying your reasoning.

callouts.p: In 'show that' questions, your final line of working must explicitly match the expression printed in the question prompt.

analogy.p: Think of an equation as a specialized lock that only opens with one exact key (the single solution, e.g., x = 5). Think of an identity as a master keycard that opens every door in the building no matter which room you try (true for all numbers). Where the analogy breaks down is that identities can involve infinite numbers of variables, whereas a physical building has a finite number of doors.

terms.d: A mathematical phrase combining numbers, variables, and operators without an equals sign.
A statement that two expressions are equal, true only for specific values of the variable.
An equation that is true for all possible values of the variables, denoted by \u2261.
Expressions that simplify to the exact same algebraic form and yield identical values for any input.
A numerical or constant quantity placed before and multiplying a variable in an expression.
Replacing numerical values in place of variables within an expression or equation.
An example that disproves a statement or identity.
Multiplying out brackets to write an expression without brackets.
Rewriting an expression as a product of its factors by reversing expansion.
A fixed numerical value that does not change within an expression.
A symbol, usually a letter like x, representing an unknown or changing number.
An expression consisting of variables and coefficients involving only addition, subtraction, and non-negative integer exponentiation.

mistakes.w: Treating an identity like an equation and trying to 'solve' for x.
mistakes.r: Recognise that identities are true for all x, so you manipulate and simplify rather than solve.

mistakes.w: Writing an equals sign (=) when proving an algebraic identity.
mistakes.r: Use the triple bar symbol (\u2261) to denote strict mathematical identity.

mistakes.w: Concluding two expressions are equivalent after testing only x = 1.
mistakes.r: Testing numbers only shows consistency; full algebraic expansion is required for proof.

mistakes.w: Expanding (x + 4)^2 as x^2 + 16.
mistakes.r: Correctly expand as x^2 + 8x + 16, including the middle cross-terms.

mistakes.w: Saying an equation has infinite solutions.
mistakes.r: Linear equations have one solution; identities have infinite solutions.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to distribute a negative sign when expanding brackets like -3(x - 4).
mistakes.r: Multiply -3 by -4 to get +12.

mistakes.w: Confusing 'solve' and 'simplify' command words in exam questions.
mistakes.r: Solve finds unknown values; simplify combines terms without an equals sign.

exam.q: Explain why 3x + 2 = 14 is an equation and not an identity.
model: It is only true for one specific value of x (x = 4).
An identity is true for all values of x.
exam.tip: Keep explanations concise, directly contrasting the definitions.

exam.q: Show that 4(2x + 3) + 5 is equivalent to 8x + 17.
model: Add 5 to get 8x + 17, which matches the right hand side.
exam.tip: Show every intermediate step of expansion clearly.

exam.q: State whether x^2 - 9 \u2261 (x - 3)(x + 3) is true or false. Give a reason.
model: Expanding the right side gives x^2 + 3x - 3x - 9, which simplifies to x^2 - 9.
exam.tip: Recognise the difference of two squares instantly.

exam.q: A student claims that (x + 5)^2 \u2261 x^2 + 25. Show by substitution that this claim is false.
model: Left side: (2 + 5)^2 = 49; Right side: 2^2 + 25 = 29. Since 49 \u2260 29, it is false.
exam.tip: Clearly state the chosen value of x and evaluate both sides separately.

exam.q: Which of the following is an identity? Circle your answer: A) 2x = 6, B) x + 2 = 2 + x, C) x^2 = 4, D) 3x - 1 = 8.
exam.tip: Look for commutative property or statements true for all numbers.
Watch out for negative signs when expanding the second bracket.

exam.q: Find the values of a and b given that 5x + 7 \u2261 a(x + 1) + b.
model: Expand right side: ax + a + b.
Equate constants: a + b = 7, so 5 + b = 7 \u21d2 b = 2.
exam.tip: Match coefficients of identical powers of x on both sides.

exam.q: Explain the difference between an equation and an identity using mathematical terminology.
model: An equation is satisfied by specific values of the variable.
An identity holds true for all values of the variable.
exam.tip: Use mark-scheme keywords like 'satisfied by' and 'holds true'.

exam.q: Determine if 2(3x - 4) + 6 is equivalent to 6x - 2.
model: Simplify to 6x - 2, so yes they are equivalent.
exam.tip: Always conclude with a clear statement answering the question.

worked.q: Prove that the expression (x + 4)(x + 2) is equivalent to x^2 + 6x + 8.
steps: Step 1: Multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second bracket (FOIL method).
Step 2: Expand to get x^2 + 2x + 4x + 8.
Step 3: Collect the like terms +2x and +4x to obtain +6x.
Step 4: Conclude that (x + 4)(x + 2) \u2261 x^2 + 6x + 8.

worked.q: Find the missing integers p and q in the identity: 3x - 12 \u2261 3(x - p) + q.
steps: Step 1: Expand the right side of the identity: 3(x - p) + q \u2261 3x - 3p + q.
Step 2: Compare the constant term from the expanded form (-3p + q) with the constant term in the original expression (-12).
Step 3: Since the x coefficients match (3 = 3), equate the constants: -3p + q = -12. Wait, let us expand standard form: 3(x - 4) = 3x - 12, so p = 4 and q = 0.

maths_eduqas_f.1.6.summary: Functions act as mathematical machines that take a specific input value, apply a given algebraic operation, and produce an output value. Understanding how to interpret simple expressions as functions allows us to evaluate them for given numbers and work backwards from outputs to find unknown inputs. This foundational concept bridges algebraic expressions and graphical representations, providing a clear pathway for solving multi-step mathematical problems.

core.p: A function machine is a visual representation of an algebraic expression, showing how an input is transformed into an output through a series of operations. The input enters the machine, undergoes the specified mathematical operations in the correct order, and emerges as the output value.
bullets: Inputs represent the starting values substituted into the function.
Operations inside the machine show the mathematical steps to perform.
Outputs represent the final calculated result of the function.
Function machines reinforce the correct order of operations (BIDMAS).

callouts.p: A relationship or rule that assigns to each input exactly one output value.
Always read and process a function machine from left to right for forward operations.

core.p: To find the output of a function, substitute the given numerical input into the expression in place of the letter variable. Follow the standard mathematical rules of arithmetic and order of operations to calculate the final value.
bullets: Write down the given expression or function rule clearly.
Replace every instance of the variable with brackets containing the input value.
Evaluate any powers or indices first.
Perform multiplications and divisions from left to right.
Complete additions and subtractions last.

callouts.p: Always use brackets when substituting negative numbers to avoid sign errors.
Never add before multiplying unless brackets explicitly demand it.

core.p: When you are given the output of a function and need to find the original input, you must reverse the operations in reverse order. This is equivalent to solving a linear equation or finding the inverse function.
bullets: Start with the given output value on the right side.
Perform the inverse (opposite) of the last operation first.
Work backwards through the machine step by step.
Check your answer by substituting the calculated input back into the original expression.

callouts.p: Reverse both the operations AND the order in which they are applied.

core.h: Mapping Algebraic Notation to Function Machines
core.p: Algebraic expressions such as 2x + 5 can be translated directly into two-step function machines. The variable x is the input, multiplication by 2 is the first operation, and adding 5 is the second operation.
bullets: The expression 4x - 3 means: input -> multiply by 4 -> subtract 3 -> output.
The expression x / 2 + 7 means: input -> divide by 2 -> add 7 -> output.
Fractions act as division operations within the expression.
Brackets in expressions indicate operations that must be performed first.

callouts.p: A combination of numbers, letters (variables), and operational symbols without an equals sign.

core.p: In higher mathematics and later GCSE topics, functions are written using formal notation such as f(x) = 3x - 2. Here, f is the name of the function, x is the input placed inside the parentheses, and the expression on the right is the rule.
bullets: Read f(x) as 'f of x'.
Finding f(5) means substituting 5 in place of every x in the expression.
Other letters like g(x) or h(x) are also used to name different functions.
The output can be written as y or as f(x).

callouts.p: Treat f(x) exactly as you would treat y when evaluating expressions.

core.p: Many foundation exam questions feature two-step function machines where students must complete missing boxes, find missing inputs, or find missing outputs. Accuracy with basic arithmetic is essential here.
bullets: Identify whether you are moving forwards (finding output) or backwards (finding input).
Look for a complete pair of input and output numbers to test or deduce operations if needed.
Write down intermediate values clearly during multi-step calculations.

callouts.p: Be extremely careful when subtracting negative numbers or dividing across negative integers.

core.p: Substituting negative numbers into expressions requires careful attention to signs. Multiplying two negative numbers gives a positive result, while adding a negative number is equivalent to subtraction.
bullets: Negative x negative = positive.
Positive x negative = negative.
Example: if f(x) = 5 - 2x, and input is -3, then f(-3) = 5 - 2(-3) = 5 + 6 = 11.

callouts.p: Subtracting a negative number is the same as adding the corresponding positive number.

core.p: Functions are frequently used to model real-world scenarios, such as mobile phone tariffs, taxi fares, or temperature conversions. The input represents a real quantity (like hours or miles), and the output represents the cost or resulting measure.
bullets: A taxi charge of £3 plus £2 per mile is written as the function f(x) = 2x + 3.
Here x represents the number of miles travelled.
The output f(x) represents the total fare in pounds.

callouts.p: Always check if final answers in real-life contexts require currency or measurement units.

core.p: Sometimes a function applies multiple operations involving brackets or powers. For foundation tier, these typically involve brackets like 3(x + 4), meaning input -> add 4 -> multiply by 3.
bullets: Brackets force the inner operation to happen before the outer operation.
In 3(x + 4), addition happens first because it is enclosed inside the brackets.
Always follow the instruction dictated by the function machine layout.

callouts.p: Operations inside brackets take precedence over external operations.

core.p: Checking your work in function questions takes only a few seconds and guarantees marks. Always take your calculated input, run it forward through the function machine or expression, and confirm it generates the exact output given in the question.
bullets: Substitute the final answer back into the original expression.
Verify that arithmetic calculations balance on both sides.
Ensure all intermediate steps are clearly shown on the examination paper.

callouts.p: Make checking your substitution values a mandatory final step for every algebra question.

analogy.p: Think of a function as a factory assembly line machine. Raw materials (the input x) enter on a conveyor belt. The first station welds a piece on (adds a number), and the second station paints it (multiplies by a number). The finished product coming off the end of the belt is the output. If you want to work backwards from a finished painted product to find what raw metal piece was used, you have to un-paint it and un-weld it in exact reverse order. Where this analogy breaks down is that physical manufacturing processes can damage materials or produce waste, whereas mathematical functions always produce a single, exact, repeatable output for every unique input.

terms.d: A rule or relationship that pairs each input value with exactly one output value.
The starting value substituted into an expression or function.
The resulting value produced after applying the function operations to the input.
A diagrammatic representation of a function showing inputs, operations, and outputs.
An operation that reverses the effect of another operation (e.g., addition and subtraction).
To replace a variable letter with a given numerical value.
A letter used to represent an unknown or changing number in an expression.
A combination of terms, numbers, and variables without an equals sign.
A standardized way of writing functions, such as f(x) = 2x + 3.
The process of calculating the numerical value of an expression for a given input.
The rules (BIDMAS/BODMAS) dictating the sequence in which calculations must be performed.
A function where the variable has a power of 1, producing a straight-line graph.
The matching of elements from an input set to an output set.

mistakes.w: Adding before multiplying when evaluating an expression like 3x + 4 with x = 2, getting 3(2 + 4) = 18.
mistakes.r: Follow BIDMAS: multiply first to get 6 + 4 = 10.

mistakes.w: Reversing operations when working backwards but keeping them in the original forward order.
mistakes.r: Reverse both the operations AND the order in which they are performed.

mistakes.w: Ignoring negative signs when substituting a negative input into an algebraic term.
mistakes.r: Use brackets around negative substitution values, e.g., -2(-4) = +8.

mistakes.w: Writing an algebraic expression with an equals sign when asked for an expression.
mistakes.r: Expressions do not have equals signs; equations do.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to apply the operation to all parts of a bracketed term.
mistakes.r: Expand brackets fully before evaluating if necessary, or follow bracket priority strictly.

mistakes.w: Confusing the input x with the output y in function machine diagrams.
mistakes.r: Inputs always enter on the left and outputs emerge on the right.

mistakes.w: Incorrectly inverting subtraction as subtraction when working backwards.
mistakes.r: The inverse of subtracting a number is adding that same number.

exam.tip: Show both steps of your calculation clearly.

exam.q: Here is a function machine: Input -> Add 6 -> Multiply by 2 -> Output. Find the input when the output is 20.
exam.tip: Remember to reverse both the operations and their order.

exam.q: A function is given by f(x) = 5x - 3. Find the value of f(4).
exam.tip: Substitute 4 in place of x and apply multiplication before subtraction.

exam.q: Here is a function machine: Input -> Square -> Add 7 -> Output. Find the output when the input is -4.
exam.tip: Squaring any negative number always results in a positive number.

exam.q: A function is defined as g(x) = 3(x + 5). Find the value of g(2).
exam.tip: Calculate the value inside the brackets first.

exam.q: Here is a function machine: Input -> Divide by 3 -> Add 4 -> Output. Find the input when the output is 10.
exam.tip: Work backwards: subtract 4 then multiply by 3.

exam.q: Given the expression 7 - 2x, find its value when x = -3.
exam.tip: Take care with the double negative when multiplying -2 by -3.

exam.q: A hire car company uses the function C(d) = 2.5d + 40 to calculate the cost £C for d miles driven. Find the cost of driving 120 miles.
exam.tip: Substitute 120 for d and evaluate using correct multiplication.

exam.q: A function machine gives the output y for input x as: x -> Multiply by 6 -> Subtract 8 -> y. Write this relationship as an algebraic formula for y in terms of x.
exam.tip: Translate each step of the machine directly into algebraic symbols.

exam.q: The output of a function is 35. The function is f(x) = 4x + 3. Work out the input x.
exam.tip: Set up an equation or work backwards using inverse operations.

worked.q: A function machine multiplies the input by 5 and then subtracts 3. (a) Find the output when the input is 7. (b) Find the input when the output is 32.
steps: For part (a), substitute input 7 into the machine: 7 x 5 = 35, then 35 - 3 = 32.
For part (b), work backwards from output 32: add 3 to get 35, then divide by 5 to get 7.
Check part (b) by running 7 forward: 7 x 5 = 35, 35 - 3 = 32 (correct).

worked.q: Given the function f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 5, evaluate the function when (a) x = 3, (b) x = -2.
steps: For (a) where x = 3: substitute 3 -> (3)^2 - 4(3) + 5 = 9 - 12 + 5 = 2.
For (b) where x = -2: substitute -2 using brackets -> (-2)^2 - 4(-2) + 5 = 4 + 8 + 5 = 17.
Ensure all squaring of negative numbers and multiplication signs are strictly evaluated.

maths_eduqas_f.1.15.summary: Simultaneous linear equations involve finding a pair of unknown values that satisfy two equations at the same time. We solve them algebraically using elimination or substitution by matching coefficients to cancel out one variable. Graphically, the exact point where two straight lines intersect represents the simultaneous solution to both equations.

core.p: Simultaneous linear equations are a pair of equations containing two unknown variables, usually x and y. A solution is a single pair of values for x and y that makes both equations true at the same time. In Foundation tier Eduqas exams, these are typically presented with integer coefficients and solved by aligning the equations.
bullets: Two equations with two unknowns are needed to find unique values for both.
The solution can be written as coordinate pairs or explicit values for x and y.
Checking your answer by substituting both values back into both original equations guarantees 100% accuracy.
Linear means the equations form straight lines when plotted on a Cartesian coordinate plane.

callouts.p: Two or more equations containing common unknown variables that are solved together to find a common solution.

core.p: When the coefficients of one variable are identical in both equations, you can eliminate that variable by subtracting the entire second equation from the first equation. This is often called the 'same sign, subtract' rule.
bullets: Ensure both equations are arranged in the standard form Ax + By = C.
Check which variable has matching numerical coefficients and identical signs.
Subtract equation 2 from equation 1 vertically, term by term.
Solve the resulting single-variable linear equation for the remaining unknown.

callouts.p: If the signs of the matching coefficients are both positive or both negative, you must subtract the equations.

core.p: When the coefficients of a variable are numerical opposites (one is positive and the other is negative), you eliminate that variable by adding the two equations together. This is the 'different signs, add' rule.
bullets: Align the terms of both equations vertically.
Identify the variable with opposite signs in front of its coefficients, e.g., +3y and -3y.
Add the two equations together term by term to eliminate that variable.
The resulting equation will contain only one variable, which is straightforward to solve.

callouts.p: If the coefficients have opposite signs (+ and -), add the equations together to eliminate the variable.

core.p: Often, neither variable has matching coefficients. To use elimination, you must multiply one or both equations by a constant integer so that one of the variables has matching coefficients.
bullets: Choose which variable is easiest to match, looking for lowest common multiples.
Multiply every single term in the chosen equation by the scaling factor.
Do not forget to multiply the constant term on the right-hand side.
Proceed with standard elimination by addition or subtraction.

callouts.p: Students frequently multiply only the x and y terms and forget to multiply the number on the far right.

core.h: Method 4: Back-Substitution to Find the Second Variable
core.p: Once you have solved for your first variable, you must find the value of the second variable. This process is called back-substitution and requires substituting your known value into either of the original equations.
bullets: Take the numerical value found for your first variable.
Substitute it in place of that letter in the simpler of the two original equations.
Rearrange the resulting linear equation to solve for the second unknown.
Always substitute into the other equation as a check to confirm your working.

callouts.p: Always substitute back into the equation with smaller numbers or fewer negative signs to reduce calculation errors.

core.p: Every linear equation represents a straight line on a graph. When you solve simultaneous equations, you are mathematically finding the exact point where the two straight lines cross or intersect.
bullets: Plot both linear equations accurately on a set of axes using a table of values or gradient-intercept methods.
The coordinates (x, y) of the intersection point give the simultaneous solution.
If the lines are parallel, they never intersect, meaning there are no solutions.
Non-calculator papers may ask you to read off approximate solutions from a given sketch or drawn graph.

callouts.p: The unique coordinate pair (x, y) where two plotted lines cross, representing the solution to both equations.

bullets: Locate the exact intersection point of the two curves or lines.
Draw dashed perpendicular lines down to the x-axis and across to the y-axis.
Estimate decimal values carefully based on the scale of the grid divisions.
State your approximate coordinates clearly as required by the question.

callouts.p: Always place a physical ruler on your exam paper to trace accurately from the intersection point to the axes.

core.h: Setting Up Simultaneous Equations from Context
core.p: Word problems often require you to translate a real-life situation into a pair of simultaneous equations before solving them. This tests your ability to form algebraic expressions from English sentences.
bullets: Define two clear variables representing the unknown items, such as let c = cost of a coffee and t = cost of a tea.
Write one equation for each piece of information or transaction given in the prompt.
Check that you have two distinct linear equations with the same two variables.
Solve using elimination or substitution as standard.

callouts.p: Always start by writing down what your letters represent, e.g., 'Let x be an adult ticket and y be a child ticket'.

core.p: Eduqas papers follow predictable patterns for simultaneous equations. Foundation questions usually feature integer coefficients with straightforward elimination, carrying 3 or 4 marks.
bullets: Standard 3-mark question: Solve 3x + 2y = 13 and x + 2y = 7.
Standard 4-mark question requiring scaling: Solve 2x + 5y = 19 and 3x + 2y = 11.
Contextual problem: Buying items at a cafe or tickets for an event.
Graphical question: Estimating intersection coordinates from plotted lines.

callouts.p: Never rely solely on mental arithmetic or calculator built-in solvers; method marks require clear algebraic steps.

core.p: A hallmark of a grade 9 student is checking their work before moving on. Verification takes less than 30 seconds and eliminates silly arithmetic slips.
bullets: Substitute both x and y values into the first original equation to check the left and right sides match.
Substitute the exact same values into the second original equation.
If both equations balance correctly, your solution is guaranteed to be correct.
If one equation fails, re-examine your back-substitution step first.

callouts.p: Always test your final x and y values in the equation you did NOT use for back-substitution.

analogy.t: Weighing Mystery Parcels on Two Scales
analogy.p: Imagine you have two different types of mystery parcels, apples (x) and bananas (y). You put combinations of them on two different weighing scales and record the total weights. By comparing what happens when you subtract one scale from the other, the heavier fruit cancels out, leaving you with the exact weight of a single fruit. This is precisely what elimination does algebraically! The analogy breaks down if weights are negative, as physical parcels cannot have negative mass, whereas algebraic variables easily can.

terms.d: A set of equations with two or more variables that are solved together.
The process of removing one variable by adding or subtracting equations.
Replacing a variable with its known numerical value or equivalent expression.
The number written directly in front of a variable term.
The exact point where two graphical lines cross each other.
Substituting a solved variable back into an equation to find the second variable.
An algebraic equation in which the highest power of the variable is 1.
A pair of numbers (x, y) that locate a specific point on a grid.
Equations that share at least one common solution pair.
Multiplying all terms in an equation by a constant factor.
An unknown quantity represented by a letter.
Values for the unknowns that satisfy all given equations simultaneously.

mistakes.w: Subtracting equations when coefficients have opposite signs
mistakes.r: Always add equations when coefficients have different signs (+ and -).

mistakes.w: Multiplying only the variable terms when scaling an equation
mistakes.r: Multiply every term in the entire equation, including the constant on the right.

mistakes.w: Stopping after finding only the first variable
mistakes.r: You must always perform back-substitution to find the second variable.

mistakes.w: Mixing up x and y coordinates in the final answer statement
mistakes.r: Clearly state both x = ... and y = ... alongside coordinate notation if requested.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to distribute a negative sign during subtraction
mistakes.r: Be extremely careful with signs when subtracting a negative term.

mistakes.w: Guessing numbers instead of using formal algebra
mistakes.r: Foundation mark schemes award method marks for proper algebraic steps, not guesses.

mistakes.w: Reading graph axes incorrectly due to misinterpreting grid subdivisions
mistakes.r: Check the value of each individual grid square before estimating coordinates.

exam.q:
Solve the simultaneous equations:
5x + y = 19
2x + y = 10
model: Substituting to find y: 2(3) + y = 10 => y = 4
exam.tip: Since both y coefficients are +1, subtract the equations directly to eliminate y.

exam.q:
Solve algebraically:
3x + 2y = 13
x + 2y = 7
model: Subtracting the second equation from the first: 2x = 6
exam.tip: Check your answer: 3(3) + 2(2) = 9 + 4 = 13. Correct!

exam.q:
Solve the simultaneous equations:
2x + 3y = 18
x - 3y = 3
model: Substitute x = 7 into second equation: 7 - 3y = 3 => 3y = 4 => y = 4/3 or 1.33
exam.tip: Look out for opposite signs (+3y and -3y)—always ADD in this case.

exam.q:
A cinema sells adult tickets (a) and child tickets (c).
2 adults and 3 children cost £34.
4 adults and 1 child cost £38.
Form and solve simultaneous equations to find the cost of an adult ticket and a child ticket.
model: Substitute a = 8 into Eq 2: 4(8) + c = 38 => 32 + c = 38 => c = 6
exam.tip: Scale one equation so that the coefficient of c matches before eliminating.

exam.q: Estimate the solution to the simultaneous equations represented by the intersection of two lines on a graph where the lines cross at x = 2.4 and y = 5.1.
exam.tip: Ensure your estimates fall within the acceptable examiner tolerance range for graph reading.

exam.q:
Solve the simultaneous equations:
4x + 2y = 16
3x - 2y = 5
model: Add equations because y coefficients are +2 and -2: 7x = 21
exam.tip: Adding equations with opposite signs eliminates the y variable immediately.

exam.q: Explain why the simultaneous equations y = 2x + 4 and y = 2x - 5 have no solutions.
model: Both lines have the same gradient (gradient = 2)
The y-intercepts are different (4 and -5), meaning the lines are parallel and never intersect
exam.tip: Parallel lines have identical gradients and will never meet.

exam.q:
Solve algebraically:
5x + 3y = 29
4x + 3y = 26
exam.tip: Fractions in final answers are completely normal; do not panic if numbers do not divide evenly.

exam.q:
Solve the simultaneous equations:
2x + y = 11
x - y = 1
model: Substitute x = 4 into x - y = 1 => 4 - y = 1 => y = 3
exam.tip: Adding equations eliminates +y and -y instantly.

exam.q:
A shop sells pens (p) and notebooks (n).
3p + n = 5.50
p + n = 2.50
Find the cost of one pen and one notebook.
model: Substitute p = 1.50 into second equation: 1.50 + n = 2.50 => n = 1.00
exam.tip: Subtracting matching coefficients for n eliminates it directly.

worked.q:
Solve the simultaneous equations algebraically:
2x + y = 7
3x - y = 8
steps: Step 1: Check the coefficients of y. Equation 1 has +y and Equation 2 has -y.
Step 2: Since the signs are different, add Equation 1 and Equation 2 together: (2x + 3x) + (y + -y) = 7 + 8.
Step 3: Simplify to get 5x = 15.
Step 4: Solve for x by dividing by 5: x = 3.
Step 5: Substitute x = 3 back into Equation 1: 2(3) + y = 7.
Step 6: Simplify: 6 + y = 7, so y = 1.

worked.q:
Solve the simultaneous equations algebraically:
3x + 2y = 16
x + 4y = 22
steps: Step 1: Notice coefficients do not match. Multiply Equation 2 by 3 so the x coefficients match: 3(x + 4y = 22) becomes 3x + 12y = 66.

Step 2: Write Equation 1 and the new scaled equation together:
3x + 2y = 16
3x + 12y = 66
Step 3: Subtract the first equation from the scaled equation: (3x - 3x) + (12y - 2y) = 66 - 16.
Step 4: Simplify: 10y = 50, so y = 5.
